title: The Silver Car

pages.text:
The headlights cut through the dusk like two angry eyes. Juno froze. The silver car was parked right where they had been digging, its chrome bumper gleaming in the fading light. The door slid open, and Mr. Cornelius Grubb stepped out. He smoothed his tiny mustache and looked at them with a smile that didn’t reach his eyes.

"Well, well," he said, his voice smooth as oil. "Little scavengers. I see you’ve been poking around my property."

Juno stepped in front of Teo. She touched her pocket. The Moon Pearl hummed against her fingers, a warm, rhythmic beat. "It’s not your property," she said. Her voice shook, but only a little. "It’s a wreck. It’s been here for a hundred years."

Grubb tilted his head. "A hundred years of neglect," he said. "But I have offers that are very good. I’m talking about a full renovation. New paint. New docks. Maybe a parking lot where that old lighthouse stands. It’s a shame to let it rot."

He looked at Juno, really looked at her, and his gaze dropped to her hand. "And that? Is that a pretty pearl?"

Juno’s heart hammered. She pulled her hand behind her back. "It’s a rock," she lied.

"Is it?" Grubb took a step closer. He smelled of expensive cologne and stale coffee. "I have a collection. I’d pay a fair price for a unique find. For a girl who wants to be home in time for dinner."

Teo shifted his weight. His tool belt clinked. "My dad says you can’t buy history, Mr. Grubb."

"History is expensive, son," Grubb said softly. "But the future is convenient."
pages.image: A tall man in a shiny grey suit smiles politely at a girl in a yellow raincoat and a boy in a green cap near a silver car in the twilight.

pages.text:
Juno didn’t want to be greedy. She didn’t want to sell Grandma’s secret to a man who wanted to build mini-golf holes on sacred ground. But she also didn’t want to be rude.

"No, thank you," she said. "We’re just cleaning up."

Grubb sighed, a long, theatrical sound. "Disappointing. I suppose I’ll just have to file the paperwork tomorrow. The harbor is mine, legally speaking, as soon as the banks approve the loan." He paused, his eyes narrowing. "Be careful out there, children. The mud is deep."

He got back into the car. The engine purred, a low, predatory growl. As the car pulled away, the headlights swept over the mudflats, illuminating the dark water and the silent boats.

Teo let out a breath he seemed to have been holding for an hour. "Did you see that?"

"See what?" Juno asked, her legs feeling like jelly.

"The door," Teo said. He pointed a shaking finger at the retreating silver car. "The driver’s side door. There’s a mark."

Juno squinted. The car was already a speck in the distance, but in that final flash of light, she saw it. A small, dark scrape on the silver paint. It wasn’t a dent. It was a missing piece. A tooth-shaped void.

"It looks like a gear," Juno whispered.

"A gear?" Teo adjusted his round glasses. "Grubb’s office is full of clocks. I saw it once when I dropped a wrench. He had a brass gear on his desk. Big one. Heavy."

Juno’s blood went cold. The Moon Gear. It was missing from the Tide Clock.

"He took it," she said. The words fell out of her mouth before she could catch them. "He took it from the lighthouse."

Teo stared at her. "That’s... that’s a big accusation, Juno."

"Look at the car," she insisted. "Why would a developer have a mark on his car that looks exactly like the missing part of the sea’s heart?"
pages.image: A close-up of a silver car door in the dusk, showing a distinct tooth-shaped scratch or missing piece of paint, with a boy in a green cap pointing at it.

pages.text:
"Maybe it’s a scratch from a key," Teo suggested, though he didn’t sound convinced.

"Maybe," Juno said. She felt a strange mix of anger and fear. If Grubb had the Moon Gear, he didn’t know what it was. He thought it was an antique. But he had it. And he wanted to buy the harbor.

"Why does he want the harbor?" Teo asked.

"Money," Juno said. "He thinks the tide is dead. He thinks the land is worth more as a parking lot than a harbor. If the tide comes back, the land is worth more, but he wants it cheap. He wants it broken."

Teo looked at the mud, then at the sky. "So we fix it. We get the other keys. We put the gear back."

"We have to," Juno said. "But we can’t let him know we know."

They turned to leave, but a strange sound stopped them. A high-pitched squeak. Then a muffled thud.

Biscuit, Grandpa’s fat orange cat with the chewed left ear, was standing in the middle of the road. But he wasn’t looking at them. He was looking at the silver car, which had stopped again a few feet ahead.

"Get away from there, Biscuit!" Juno hissed.

Biscuit hissed back. He batted at the air near the car’s rear bumper. Then, with a confused look, he jumped up and squeezed himself into the gap between the car and the curb. It was a tight squeeze. The fat cat wriggled, his orange fur fluffing up, and slipped under the chassis.

"Did he just... enter the car?" Teo asked.

"No," Juno said, her stomach dropping. "He went under it. And now he’s stuck."

They ran to the car. Biscuit’s eyes were visible under the bumper, wide and green. He was trapped in the tight space between the undercarriage and the mud, his tail twitching in irritation.

"Mr. Grubb!" Teo called out. "There’s a cat under your car!"

Grubb rolled down his window. He looked annoyed. "I don’t have time for animals. I have a meeting in ten minutes."

"He’s stuck!" Juno shouted.

Grubb sighed. "Fine. Give me a moment." He stepped out, not to help, but to check his watch.
pages.image: A fat orange cat with a chewed left ear peeking out from under a silver car, looking annoyed, while a girl in a yellow raincoat and a boy in a green cap look on with worry.

pages.text:
"Can you help us?" Juno asked, trying to keep her voice steady.

Grubb looked at Biscuit, then at them. "I’ll call a professional. It’s safer that way."

"No!" Juno said. "He’s fine. He just needs a nudge."

Grubb raised an eyebrow. "You want to get under my car? In the mud?"

"We can manage," Teo said. He rolled up his sleeves.

Juno knelt down. She didn’t want to touch the car. She didn’t want to be near Grubb. But Biscuit was her friend. And Biscuit looked back at her with a face of pure disdain.

"Go on, Biscuit," she whispered. "Out."

Biscuit meowed, a sound like a rusty hinge. He tried to back out, but his back legs got tangled in the mud. He stuck.

"Teo, get his tail," Juno said.

Teo knelt down, his knees sinking into the soft earth. He reached under the car. "It’s tight," he muttered. "I can barely see."

"Push him forward," Juno instructed. "Gently."

Teo pushed. Biscuit squirmed. For a second, nothing happened. Then, with a squeak of protest, the fat orange cat popped out from under the chassis, landing on his feet with a thump. He shook himself off, spraying a fine mist of mud over Teo’s green cap.

Teo froze. A single drop of brown mud sat on the brim of his cap.

"Teo," Juno said slowly.

Teo looked at his cap. He looked at Biscuit, who was licking his paw with an air of superiority.

"I’m getting mud off my cap," Teo said quietly.

Grubb, who had been watching, snorted. "Cats are messy creatures. I’m glad I’m not a pet owner."

Juno stood up. She wiped her hands on her yellow raincoat. "Thank you, Mr. Grubb. For stopping."

"It’s not a problem," Grubb said, checking his watch again. "But do be careful. The tide is low. The mud is deceptive."

He got back into the car. The engine started. But this time, he didn’t drive away. He sat in the car, the engine idling, the headlights cutting into the dark.
pages.image: A boy in a green cap with a spot of mud on it, looking shocked, while a fat orange cat stands nearby looking clean and dignified, and a man in a grey suit watches from a car window.

pages.text:
Juno stared at the car. Why was he staying?

"Juno," Teo whispered. "He’s not leaving."

Grubb rolled down the window again. He didn’t look at them. He was looking at the lighthouse in the distance. The dark silhouette of the tower loomed against the twilight.

"I saw you climb it," Grubb said. His voice was low. "Two days ago. I have cameras in the bay. For security. For my future... parking lot."

Juno’s heart stopped.

"I didn’t care," he continued. "Who cares about a few kids playing in a ruin? But today, I saw you take something from the wreck. I saw the light. A blue light. Unnatural."

Juno’s hand went to her pocket. The Moon Pearl was pulsing. She could feel it.

"I’m not a thief," she said. "It belongs to the sea."

"Everything belongs to the highest bidder," Grubb said. "And the sea is gone. It’s dead. You’re just picking bones."

He started the car. The tires spun in the mud, throwing dirt over their boots.

"Wait!" Juno yelled. "If you take the gear, the tide won’t come back. Everyone will lose their homes. The fish will die. The boats will rot."

Grubb’s head turned, just slightly. "That’s a lot of pressure for two children."

He drove away. The silver car disappeared into the night, leaving only the smell of exhaust and the sound of the wind.

Juno stood still. Her hands were shaking.

"He knows," she said. "He knows we have it."

Teo took off his muddy cap and looked at it. "He has cameras. He knows where we are. He knows what we’re doing."

Juno looked at the lighthouse. The dark shape of it seemed to lean toward them, waiting.

"Then we’re faster," she said. "We have to get the second key. Tonight."

Biscuit yawned and walked away, unbothered by the drama.
pages.image: A girl in a yellow raincoat and a boy in a green cap standing in the mud, looking up at a dark lighthouse in the distance, with the silhouette of a silver car driving away in the background.

summary: Mr. Grubb confronts Juno and Teo at the wreck, offering money for the Moon Pearl and revealing he has cameras that saw them at the lighthouse. Teo notices a tooth-shaped mark on Grubb's silver car, confirming he stole the Moon Gear. Biscuit gets stuck under the car, forcing a brief, tense interaction where Grubb hints he knows about their activities and believes the sea is dead.
